content: Unique identifiers are often recorded in logbooks or registers and serve as person-centered health record identifiers. These identifiers are typically used across healthcare facilities to improve the continuity of care for individuals, facilitate appointment scheduling and follow-ups, and enhance the linkage between clinical care and other services such as laboratories and pharmacies. They also improve the confidentiality of health data. At the program or service level, identifiers are used across multiple facilities managed by the same organization or provider, whether in the public or private sector. These identifiers may be disease-specific, such as those for HIV or tuberculosis programs, or location-based, such as those for hospitals or community facilities. The use of unique identifiers at this level improves the linkage between testing and treatment, ensures continuity and transferability of care when patients move between facilities or settings, reduces loss to follow-up, and minimizes duplication of health records for the same individual. However, facilityand program-level identifiers have limitations. They provide unique identification only within specific facilities or programs, which can lead to duplication of records. National-level identifiers, on the other hand, are designed for use across all public health facilities in a country. These identifiers may be part of a broader national system that includes civil registration, vital event registries, syndromic surveillance, or even non-health-related uses such as social services or voter registration. In regions where individuals receive care across national borders or participate in international research studies, identifiers may extend to neighboring countries. National-level unique health identifiers enhance the capacity and reach of facilityand program-level identifiers. Their benefits include the ability to create comprehensive, longitudinal health records that track service use, costs, and outcomes; improved linkage between HIV and other services; easier referrals and reimbursements; better case surveillance through linking sentinel events for the same person; enhanced data linkage for program management and population-based research; accurate de-duplication of aggregate data; integration of information from different service providers and systems; improved data quality; and better management of programs, services, and consumables like drugs and diagnostics. Unique identifiers act as the glue that links various data sources for patient monitoring and surveillance. They enable the translation of disparate data sources into a person-centered data repository. For example, clinical systems, laboratory records, radiology data, pharmacy records, and disease-specific registers (e.g., for antiretroviral therapy or tuberculosis) can all be linked using a shared registration number, such as a National Health Identifier (NHID). This integration facilitates person-centered monitoring and program management. The implementation and scaling up of unique identifiers require appropriate legal frameworks, policies, protocols, training, and infrastructure to ensure the privacy, confidentiality, and security of personal health information. Assigning an identifier to an individual ensures that they can be consistently and accurately identified when accessing healthcare services. This process, known as authentication, can be achieved in three ways: (1) assigning an ID card to each individual and requiring its presentation during service use; (2) using biometric data (e.g., photographs, fingerprints) stored in the record system and re-reading this data during each visit; or (3) creating an identifier from existing demographic data, such as name, date of birth, and sex, or using an existing identifier like a passport number or medical record number. The latter approach is sometimes referred to as a pseudo-identifier. A country situation assessment should evaluate the investments and benefits of using existing identifiers, such as national ID cards, versus creating new identifiers specifically for the healthcare sector. Progress in implementing unique identifiers should be measured through improvements in record linkage accuracy, de-duplication, and program benefits, with time-bound targets to support necessary investments. The transition to unique identifiers and electronic health records involves several stages. Initially, the focus is on replacing name-based records with unique identifiers in paper-based systems. In the middle stage, unique identifiers are widely used, and electronic data systems with online and offline elements are deployed. In the advanced stage, data linked by unique identifiers is integrated into fully online electronic health information systems that connect services, facilities, and community care. Key components of this transition include person identification, data security and confidentiality, data analysis and quality, and the shift from paper to electronic systems. Each stage offers benefits such as improved continuity of care, enhanced data security, and better program efficiency, but also presents risks like data security vulnerabilities and high initial infrastructure costs. Sustainability of program improvements requires robust systems for patient monitoring, linking individual data within and between facilities, and ensuring continuity of care. This includes appointment scheduling, follow-ups, and linking clinical, laboratory, and pharmacy information. Electronic health records updated in real-time further enhance the quality of care and program management.
